speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES REPORTED LAY-OFF OF 104 PILOTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Laurier asked me a question about layoffs of T.C.A. pilots. As I indicated at that time, T.C.A. took this action with considerable regret. It is, however, a problem which has had to be faced by every major air line when they switched to jet powered aircraft.
I should like to mention some of the steps taken by T.C.A. to ease the impact on those affected. Furloughing of the 104 pilots will be arranged in a progressive fashion over the

period February to August, 1961, to avoid the more difficult winter period. The company has approached other air lines to ascertain possibilities of other employment and has met with a favourable response. The company has also agreed to an earlier furlough for any pilot where this will assist in employment by another air line. Every effort will be made to assist those pilots who wish to remain with T.C.A. in a ground capacity pending recall for flight duties. Every one of the pilots affected has had three years service or less with T.C.A., but pension and other rights will be protected during furlough and pending recall to service with T.C.A.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, December 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-52 to establish a national productivity council-Mr. Hees-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
We have before us a bill which has as its purpose the setting up of a productivity council. An indication was given during the discussion yesterday that this would automatically be of benefit to the Canadian people. It was indicated also that this will be part of the government's program to overcome some of the ills of the present employment situation, and many of the workers will look on this measure as one of the methods adopted by the government to end the employment crisis.
In Canada over the years, and particularly in recent years, we have increased the productivity of many segments of our economy by leaps and bounds. However, in many cases this has done very little for large sections of the national economy. On many occasions when increased productivity does take place none of the benefit accrues to the workers and none, or very little, to the general public.
I object to the government saying that this measure is one of the solutions they are advancing in order to cope with unemployment, because it seems to me that even if we put into effect all the good which could flow from the work of this council we should still have heavy unemployment. It seems likely that the effects of this bill will be felt only in the future, and then to a very questionable extent, and that is not likely to have any beneficial effects at the present time.
This bill contains no provision to make possible the bringing of recommendations to parliament for consideration and implementation. The representatives on the council can voluntarily accept the recommendations that will benefit the group with which they are associated. I am in many instances distrustful of the use industry makes of the advances, in productivity that are achieved. In the mining industry, in which I have been engaged, productivity per man hour

Productivity Council
has increased tremendously in the last number of years. Within my memory the mining industry has undertaken a reduction in employment of approximately 30 per cent because of automation and has maintained the same level of production, but there has been little increase in wages for those miners remaining in the industry.
Let me cite one example which should be of interest to the government because of the representations made yesterday by workers in the automobile industry, but before doing so let me say the Canadian public should examine the problems arising through segments of the economy using production improvements to their own advantage. A startling illustration is the uranium industry at Elliot Lake.

The hon. member suggested that this point had never been raised. I must say that to my knowledge it has been repeatedly raised when I have been in the chair. I do not intend to unduly restrict the hon. member, but I must state that generally

what is relevant on clause 1 is a discussion of the scope of the bill, whether as drafted it is sufficient to meet the objectives contained therein. In my view that is what is relevant to discuss on clause 1.
I simply want to caution the hon. member for Timiskaming that he should not revive the debate we have concluded. That is a general principle which is well established.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I will not repeat or discuss anything the previous speaker mentioned on second reading, because that would be completely out of order and if I did so I would not be talking about the bill at all. The hon. gentleman did not say anything relevant to the bill and I could not be accused of repeating anything like that.
Many of the objectives it has been suggested this bill will accomplish will not be accomplished in fact. It is relevant to discuss this on clause 1. The bill will not produce employment except on a long range basis.
To return to my illustration of Elliot Lake, which is an example of industry using production improvements to its own advantage, the old miners' song about mining 16 tons certainly would not apply, because the miners at Elliot Lake mined 400 or 500 tons and eventually mined themselves out of a job, not in the space of 15 or 20 years but within one or two years. It is not always advantageous to increase productivity, as can be seen from this example, unless we give consideration to the important question of disposing of our surplus productivity. The bill contains no provision to meet the problem that will arise as a result of increased production.
Let me quote from a booklet entitled "Research Program on the Training of Skilled Manpower", No. 8, relating to technological changes and skilled manpower in the automobile and parts manufacturing industries, published by the Department of Labour. In a comparison of the number of employees in that industry from 1948 to 1958, we find the following statement:
Thus production, (in units) increased in the ten years approximately 36.4 per cent, in value added (not deflated) about 75 per cent, and the volume index shows an increase in production of 54.6 per cent, while total employment increased about 7 per cent. It is interesting to note that the increase in total employment obscures divergent trends with regard to direct and indirect labour. The proportion of direct labour expressed as a percentage of total employment was 82.8 per cent in 1948, 81.6 per cent in 1953, 77.0 per cent in 1954 and 72.5 per cent in 1958.
This is the interesting part:
Indeed while total employment increased 7 per cent during the period 1948-1958, the number of employees engaged! in direct production fell approximately 6] per cent during the same period.

This bill would be effective if we were to implement the recommendations of the various groups comprising the council, and if the government were to introduce marketing legislation in which the same groups would participate, and introduce means of disposing of the increased production which will worsen the present unemployment picture and heighten the causes of that problem. Consideration should be given to the disposal of present production. There are a few segments of the economy which can overproduce at the present time, and reasons should be given why this production cannot be disposed of.
I think the government has been unfair to the Canadian people. It has been unfair to those who are being asked to participate in this program, and it has been unfair to the unemployed, because in each and every pronouncement of the government there has been the implication that this council is going to supply more jobs to the Canadian people; that this is going to meet part of the problem that we have encountered because of automation and technical changes, and that something can come out of this which will produce solutions to these problems.
I suggest that this bill cannot be satisfactorily implemented unless the government does two things. First of all, in conjunction with this bill the government should set up marketing legislation which will, in the light of the national economy, handle and dispose of production as it increases from year to year. Second, the government will have to be honest with the Canadian people and tell them that this is a long range program and that it is no solution to the present problem. Unless the national economy is taken into consideration and everything is not left to private industry, this legislation can bring about an aggravation of the employment picture as we see it today.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some observations on this bill to establish a national productivity council. In doing so I will say what I have to say using as few words as possible. In this debate so far we have heard members from all parts of the country giving their approval of the principles of this legislation. I do not intend to go over ground they have covered, but I do wish to congratulate the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour on the leadership they have given in this matter. In recent weeks I have talked to many businessmen and leaders of the organized labour movement who have knowledge of this legislation, and found them unanimous in commending the government for this far-sighted bill.
Productivity Council
The bill, as I envisage it, is not one which is expected to create employment in the immediate future, but it is intended to give rise to studies and investigations as described in clause 10, which will increase the productivity of the working force of Canada and thereby raise our standards of living. I think it would be a good thing, Mr. Chairman, if we reminded ourselves that while we have many problems to solve, and there are difficulties in the economy, we in Canada live in a very prosperous country; we enjoy the second highest standard of living of any people in the world. We have only 18 million people in this country. Most of the country is under snow for five months of the year. Tens of thousands of square miles of this country are uninhabited, and much of the territory of Canada does not produce any wealth. Thousands of Canadians live and work in areas where they have a closer relationship, commercially and otherwise, with the United States, than they have with other parts of Canada, and they do not contribute to the Canadian economy as much as they do to that of the United States. Many producers live in areas which are a long way from the big Canadian markets, and to ship their goods to Canadians in other parts of the country is very costly.
I think we can all be proud of the fact that, with these limitations, Canadians have achieved a very high standard of living. The main reason for this, I think, is that we have rich natural resources, an enterprising population, and relatively less developed nations and the United States of America wanting our goods. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, there is much unwarranted criticism of that great country these days. This is the country on which the western nations, including Canada, are depending in large measure for defence against aggression. That country is our best customer; that country has invested money in Canada without which our economic growth would have been much slower. The citizens of the United States, directly and indirectly, have introduced manufacturing techniques which have brought great benefits to Canada. And so, I say, let us acknowledge that we would not be where we are today if we did not happen to be situated alongside the United States of America.
One of the general purposes of this council, as I see it, is to raise the material standards of life in this country, through working toward the objectives set out in clause 10 of the bill. In the election in the United States much was made of making America strong. In my opinion we should be concerned about making Canada strong. We must find good paying jobs for our workers. It is estimated that we must find

Productivity Council 4 million, new jobs for Canadians by 1980. Another reason why we must make Canada strong is so this country can pull its weight in maintaining military defences. I am sure every member in this house regrets that so much of our national revenue-a little less than one third-is spent for defence. We cannot shirk this responsibility, and the only way to meet it is with a strong economy.
I believe another reason for increasing productivity is to show the people in the communist and the uncommitted countries that a high standard of life can be maintained and increased in a free enterprise economy.
Finally, I think that only with greatly increased productivity can we extend our efforts to help less developed countries. I believe that here the western nations may meet their greatest test. It may well be that if we fail, the communist political and economic system may be imposed on large areas of the world which are still uncommitted. I am thinking particularly of Africa.
The council appointed under the terms of this bill will have a broad and important responsibility. I am sure it will have the cooperation of governments, members of parliament, representatives of management and organized labour and many private citizens in reaching the objectives outlined in the bill.

speechtext:
There are one or two remarks I should like to make on the benefits that will come from this council, as I see them. There has been


a good deal of discussion as to what will be done in the way of improvement of our export markets by increased efficiency in production.
However, I think one thing that has not received too much attention is the question of our own domestic markets, which in my view constitute a very important problem in Canada. We have not gained control of our own markets. We import a great many goods that I feel we could successfully produce and distribute in this country, but we have not been doing so. However, as the council is to be made up of representatives from industry, commerce, labour, agriculture, the primary industries and the general public, I believe it will be in a very strong position to encourage Canadians to buy products made in Canada. By increasing our productive efficiency the council will also help in working toward this end.
I hope the council will take this view of their powers. I think clause 10 would give them the power to undertake such a program. From time to time there have been efforts in Canada by different organizations to encourage Canadians to buy made in Canada products. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian electrical manufacturers have had very worth-while programs of trying to encourage Canadians to buy Canadian products. However, I feel that the idea has not caught on generally throughout the country. It has not been supported generally by the public or by labour, and I think it is most important that this should be done. I hope that under the powers given in clause 10, which also deals with distribution and production methods, the council will see its way clear to support a program of encouraging Canadians to buy products made in Canada. If that is done I am sure the council certainly can do a great deal to create employment.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.

I do not say that because I want them to end there. I say so simply because as I read the bill I am certain that is where their powers end. The government is doing something to tackle the important problem of improving the efficiency of Canadian industry, and in my view the more efficient our industry is the better will be the position of both industry and the nation. However, I emphasize the fact that the government is only dealing with one small part of this very great problem. If our industries are more efficient their total production will be increased, but what assurance is there that there will be a market for this increased production?
In my judgment the government is dealing with this question in a very piecemeal and inadequate fashion. By severely limiting the area of inquiry of the productivity council, the only power contained in this measure, they have already condemned the council to a limited success at the very best in a field where it is necessary for the government to take broad and immediate action. I think the minister should reply to the definite questions we are asking at this point; or if he prefers to reply to them later he should say when he wishes to do so. Certainly when members ask for answers to their questions they deserve to get them.

Mr. Chairman, the bill has been reasonably well covered by various speakers, and as a result my remarks will be quite limited at this stage. However, I think there are certain aspects of the bill that should be emphasized. In considering this productivity council it is my view that we have to keep in mind that there is a sort of three-pronged dilemma facing the country at the present time. One prong has to do with productivity itself. The second prong has to do with a market for the results of productivity. In the third place, although 90205-6-51

we have never had too much consideration of this point in the past, we certainly must give consideration to the loss of employment caused by increased productivity brought about through automation or other methods.
The bill only deals with one of these three prongs. It is geared only to increase productivity and does not give very much consideration to the other two prongs of the dilemma. It appears to me to be like an aeroplane trying to land on one wheel. If planes try to do that they find themselves in the same trouble that our economy has been confronted with over the last number of years.
Another thing that bothers me about the bill is that it appears to be just another instance of the various types of window dressing that the Prime Minister and the government subject the Canadian people to every once in a while. In fact it is beginning to look as though the Prime Minister is a serious contender with a former distinguished prime minister of this country. I should like to refer to a poem written about him by Professor F. R. Scott of McGill University, and I shall only quote two lines:
The height of his ambition
Was to pile a parliamentary committee on a royal commission.
Unfortunately this seems to be the method used in trying to deal with many of the problems of our country, the setting up of commissions and the piling of parliamentary committees on top of royal commissions.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
May I say, first of all, that without increased productivity Canada cannot possibly hope to compete in either the Canadian or foreign markets. If we cannot compete in these markets, then our workers will not have employment. Industry alone is not going to benefit from this bill, as the hon. member for Timmins has intimated. I submit that in the long run labour will benefit more from what this council will be able to do than anyone else. I want to say that through increased productivity since the end of the second world war, the standard of living has risen considerably.
It has been found from experience in the United Kingdom, Mr. Chairman, that reductions in cost can be brought about more often through greater efficiency in plant organization, in the use of machinery and in the use of fuel as well as raw materials rather than through reducing labour. This is where cost reductions have been effected rather than through reductions in labour. They have found very frequently that when these changes have been made there has been as much if not more labour required in production. In other words, as a result of these savings effected in fuel, machinery and material, labour has maintained its position and in many cases more employment has been provided.
The hon. member for Timiskaming referred to a study that was made in the automobile industry. I do not question the figures which he set forth because they were supplied by our department. I should like to say that they are factual. However, regardless of that, many other areas have had increased employment as a result of the improvement in automobile production. As examples I would cite gasoline service stations, garages, highway construction and maintenance, the tourist industry. All these areas have bene-fitted as a result of the efficiency of production and the higher level of production in the automobile industry.
The hon. member for Assiniboia raised the question of how we would get rid of these products. This, of course, raises the question of trade at home and abroad. The distributive and service industries are included in this measure, and there is no need to add consumption. The levels of consumption depend on the levels of employment and income and, in the main, government and non-government programs are involved in these things. I want to say now that industry must be efficient

to bring about higher levels of income and employment, and I am sure the productivity council will help in this regard.
There was a question as to what could be done through the establishment of the productivity council to provide employment in the short run and the long run. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that a productivity council such as we have in mind and such as is outlined in this bill can generate new employment opportunities in the short run as well as in the long run. Over the long term it is obvious that the productivity council, by fostering and promoting increased industrial efficiency through the greater use of technology, improved techniques and overall management practices, will aid many Canadian industries in the production and distribution fields to be more competitive. That is the most important thing, to be competitive and able to sell more in both the foreign and domestic markets. This, I submit, will create new employment opportunities and a higher national standard of living.
The productivity council could have a beneficial influence on employment opportunities in the short run. An increase in productivity does not only come from increased use of machinery and equipment, or new types of machinery and equipment, or from the increased use of automation, although significant productivity increases do come from the application of capital to the industrial processes. I feel that a rise in productivity will bring about efficiency, lower costs and with that combination the product will find a ready market both domestically and abroad. Second, it will give more employment, and that is the object of this bill.
I feel that these people who will be the members of this productivity council will take into consideration, because of the makeup of this council, all the aspects from the industrial viewpoint, from the labour viewpoint and from the agricultural viewpoint. I am sure that the representatives on this productivity council will bring about the desired result in producing products that will be competitive in this tremendously competitive export market with which we are faced. We must sell our products, and the only way we can sell them is to produce quality articles that will appeal to the export market at a cost that will be within the reach of the people in other countries. As a result of this, benefits will flow right down the line and employment will be generated.

Mr. Chairman, for a change I should like to thank the Minister of Labour for putting this bill in better perspective than has hitherto been the case. Certainly the

answer which the minister has just given put this measure in much better perspective than did the remarks of his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he introduced the resolution, or the remarks of the Prime Minister when he spoke twice on second reading of the bill.
I think it is quite clear that any desirable and good effects flowing from the establishment of this council, in so far as they may affect employment, will undoubtedly come indirectly through improved efficiency of industry making it more competitive in both the domestic and foreign trade fields.
Of course it is quite clear that since they come in that wholly desirable but none the less indirect way, the immediate effect of relieving unemployment does not lie in this measure. I am referring to immediate relief of the unemployment situation. It is something that will have to develop gradually as the industry becomes more efficient. I suppose no one can say precisely how long that will take, but we hope the process will continue to grow as the years go on. It would be quite wrong for anyone to assume that this meets any immediate problem of unemployment at this time. None the less, the other objective is wholly desirable and as long as the measure is understood properly, in its proper perspective, there is no objection to the true objective of the bill.
There are one or two specific questions I would like to ask the minister. As I understand it, there is no attempt by this measure to deal with the whole problem of the distribution of goods except in the physical way. That is, the whole problem of distribution is not dealt with in this bill at all and is not intended to be. My purpose in asking this question is to have the position clarified. In his remarks dealing with this subject the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke on this point in a way that is certainly capable of two or three interpretations. I refer particularly to page 566 of Hansard, where the minister is reported as having said:
The objects of the council are to foster and promote the development of improved production and distribution methods-
I take it that refers only to the improvement of distribution through the improvement of the efficiency of the industries in the distribution trades, as opposed to the larger problem of distribution. I wonder whether the minister would clarify that point?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is being made perfectly clear as this discussion goes along that the powers of the productivity council are exceedingly limited.
The Minister of Labour said a little earlier that the effect of the work of the productivity council should be to raise the level of employment and income. Of course, if this happens it will be merely an effect, a result of the work of the council, because the council obviously is not being given any powers to consider the general level of employment in the country, nor is it given any powers to consider the general level of income in the country. This is a piecemeal measure; this is a measure which is exceedingly limited in scope. As has already been said, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have painted pictures of a council that had much larger powers than in fact this council is now being given.
For the life of me I do not know why the government has not given this council the power of inquiring-and that is all the power the council has-into the whole field of consumer tastes, into the whole field of consumer income and into the whole field of national economic policy.
If this government wants to solve the problem of unemployment, if it wants to bring about full production and a full employment economy, and if at the same time it has any faith whatsoever in a council composed of the kinds of people who will be members of this council, it should not be binding the hands and feet of the council at the same time it is being established.
I say that the government has not gone nearly far enough in this measure and is not giving this council the power of inquiry which might lead to full employment. I do not know what the government is afraid of; I do not

know why it does not give this productivity council increased powers so that it might do a real job, instead of condemning it to major failure initially by limiting its powers. I have no objection to the powers that are being given to the council, but I say that those powers are inadequate and that in consequence the objective of full employment cannot be attained by this measure. It is doubtful how far the council can go in bringing about the results to which government spokesmen have referred.
I wish to ask the minister another question. I think I know the answer, but I hope, once again, that the minister may be able to persuade me that I am wrong in my conclusion. I ask the minister whether the productivity council has power to make any recommendations whatsoever to the government. I would suggest that under the terms of this measure the council has no jurisdiction to make a recommendation to the government. It can look into conditions, it can inquire into the situation, it can "promote and expedite continuing improvement in productive efficiency in the various aspects of Canadian economic activity"; it can do certain specific things, but it cannot recommend to the government. It is not in a position to advise the government as to what action should be taken by the government in these fields. I suggest that this measure should be amended in order to give the productivity council, not only the broader powers I have mentioned but also the power to come to a conclusion and, having reached a conclusion, to make a recommendation to the government.
This government is giving the council fewer powers than it has given to royal commissions. The government has been setting up an almost countless number of royal commissions which have the power of inquiry and the power to make recommendations to the government. I ask the minister if the productivity council has the right and authority to make particular recommendations to the government from time to time and, if so, in what provision of the bill is that power contained.

It seems to me that these arguments are without foundation. The real meat of the powers of the council are found in clause 10, and they are not limited to those powers which are established in the subclauses which follow. The clause states:
The objects of the council are to promote and expedite continuing improvement in productive efficiency in the various aspects of Canadian economic activity-
How much wider, how much further could the government go in order to promote what the minister has suggested is necessary? The clause goes on to say:
.. . without limiting the generality of the foregoing. the council may, in furtherance of its objects-
Then it goes on to set out what else can be done. But that first subclause is in terms as wide as it is possible to imagine, and I think it is wise to have it so. As the council, in the pursuance of its duties and functions, becomes aware of things that must be done, it need not go back to seek additional powers but finds them within the four corners of this particular clause. I think that is an ample answer to the hon. member for Ottawa West who asked the minister certain questions on this subject. The authority for what the council may wish to recommend and do is found in this clause. I do not think there is any doubt about it, and any attempt to tie the hands of the council by saying it can only do this and this and this is bound to have the result of limiting its accomplishments.
Some question has been raised as to whether the appointment of this council would have the effect of increasing employment. I think it would have precisely that effect, not necessarily today and tomorrow, but in due course. As a matter of fact, this organization should have been set up ten, or 12 or 15 years ago.

With regard to this question of employment. Surely, if as a result of increased efficiency, goods are continuously made available to the people of this country at a lower rate, there will then be available sums of money to be expended on other goods, commodities and services, as a result of which increased employment will be made available to the labour force of this country.

Obviously, these powers are specifically designed for the purpose the hon. member had in mind.
I read not so long ago about a situation on the west coast of the United States. One of the most militant of unions, the international longshoremen's union, which has had a long history of strikes and troubles, had reached an agreement with the ship owners and employers under which the employers had established a fund of some $5 million for the purpose of providing an education scheme for the union members, for making possible earlier retirement, and for supplementing other benefits. The whole purpose was to obtain the consent of the unions to the establishment of techniques of automation in connection with the loading and unloading of ships and cargoes so that fewer people could do the work in a shorter time. That is the sort of thing which I assume under the provisions of this bill will be made available to the people of this country.
