subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to follow up the answer given by the Minister of Labour to the question about the authority of the council to recommend changes in

Productivity Council
policy to the government. As I understood his answer, supported by the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River, it was to the effect that the council could do this even although it was not given authority under the objects spelled out in clause 10 of the bill. I only want to suggest to the minister with great deference that if any council financed by the taxpayers of this country as this one will be through the grant of $150,000 a year for three years were to so far exceed the powers given to it in such a basic matter as that and in such a basic way, I am sure there would be a reference in the Auditor General's report the very first year drawing the attention of parliament to the misuse of funds, to the fact that they were used for a purpose not provided for by the vote of parliament.
Surely on reflection the minister will revise his opinion. It is my own view that the council should have the authority we were discussing so that it could make recommendations to the government for the government's decision as to whether or not they would be adopted. It is clear in the bill that the council is not given that right and I do not think the minister can give the council that right by merely saying that it can use the money granted by parliament for that purpose even although it is not set out in the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT, EXERCISE OF POWERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This is perhaps the first time I have seen something emasculated even before it was born. That seems to be precisely what will occur with the productivity council. I listened with interest to the interpretation of the hon. member for Peace River with respect to clause 10. I gather the council can do anything and everything it likes because of the words "without limiting the generality of the foregoing" and because of the reference to its objects there. I assume the minister agrees with the interpretation that the council has all-embracing power and authority which is not even referred to in the measure. I wonder if the council will have authority to make recommendations not only to the government but to specific industries or specific segments of the economy concerning what they should or should not do. Does the council have this authority? Is that included in the all-embracing phraseology of clause 10? I think it is not.
I think the sole relationship between the council and various segments of the economy is to be channelled through the editorial branch of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour and perhaps even the Prime Minister may be involved in squeezing out what little substance there may be in the council's reports.
[Mr. Mcllraith. I
What is the relationship of the council to the agricultural industry? The minister should explain this before we proceed further.
Has the council any authority to tell industry what to do? No, of course not, yet the hon. member for Peace River suggested it did and the minister by maintaining his silence perhaps agreed. One could reach that conclusion. We know full well that the council has not that authority. The council has no authority to invade the files of various groups in the economy with respect to the research and development ideas they have acquired in order to disseminate that information among various segments of the economy. The council does not have that authority and the minister would be the first to say so. When we talk about this all-embracing authority we are talking through our hats. We have to colour a little the interpretation placed on this by the minister and his supporters in the government.
The minister mentioned the long range possible accomplishments with respect to employment. The council may disseminate information or foster the development of techniques which would mean that production costs could be made lower than they are now. The implication is that employment would be stimulated and consumption would increase but I think it is nonsense to piously expect that this would take place.
A professor of economics was engaged by the Eisenhower administration in the United States to study the question of why we have increasing costs of living and increasing prices of goods and commodities and at the same time a decline in employment and a condition of over-supply. The answer the professor gave which has been supported by Canadian economists is that there is in both countries a system of administered prices under which producers take the position of keeping prices as high as possible and not reflecting in lower prices the lower cost of producing the goods-in those cases where costs are lower

and keeping the margin of profit to themselves. The experience with combines in the field of price fixing indicates that lower costs are not necessarily reflected to the advantage of the consumer because of the system of administering prices through the collaboration and connivance of several groups in the same field.
It is quite obvious that this government is stretching things quite a bit because a few months ago, during the last session, this parliament, at the behest of the government and over our violent objections, endorsed and passed amendments to the Combines Investigation Act which will allow those price administrators to operate with this great freedom. What is being set up in this bill

as an objective and a hope has already been defeated by the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act which were made by this government during the last session.
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Chairman, all sorts of questions that were in our minds during the resolution stage were voiced. Even when the bill was introduced there were still questions in our minds. During the second reading we had a person who was substituting for the Minister of Trade and Commerce introduced the legislation, namely the Prime Minister, and he certainly was not enlightening as to the objectives that this particular council was going to accomplish. He was extremely eloquent and emotional, as he is on many occasions, but enlightening, no.
Now we have the Minister of Labour, and this is the first opportunity we have had of questioning the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, in this committee. The minister has been far more enlightening about what may or may not occur under this bill than either his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Prime Minister himself. To this extent it is a change for which we are thankful. Incidentally, we wish more cabinet ministers would act in the same way and would be as open and as sincere as the Minister of Labour. As I say, the minister has been enlightening to some extent, and has admitted that there are a number of weaknesses in the bill. This is appreciated.
As more and more questions are asked, more criticisms made and answers given to the questions and criticisms, I wonder whether I should be asked to participate in squandering at least $150,000 a year of the taxpayers' money on something which is going to accomplish practically nothing in the immediate future in so far as promoting employment is concerned, and relatively little in the long haul ahead unless some pretty drastic changes are made in the structure of the council.

I think the minister is quite right when he points out that the increased productivity in itself will not be as beneficial to the country as we would like it to be unless, as the minister properly pointed out, we have markets for the increased productivity. That, I think, is a very important matter. Most efficient businesses nowadays have been taught to call in what are known as efficiency experts who time each operation with a stop watch and who clock the staff to see whether one cannot knock off minutes from certain operations. This is the same sort of suggestion. When private business increases its productivity or produces its products more economically, those products are useless to anyone unless the producer has a market for the product. If the productivity
Productivity Council
council is to succeed in its objectives it should also be concerned about markets for the product of this elaborate system or organization of efficiency experts.
Perhaps the minister can point out to us what is in the bill to deal with the outlets, the markets for this increased and more economical productivity. I do not think this should be merely an exercise, an exploratory council which will be set up to make reports. In a measure of this kind I should like to see some indication of where all this increased productivity will go. If it can be sold, fine. Then we shall have employment for our people. If this increased productivity is simply to remain on the shelves and not be sold, then we shall have advanced nothing.
I should have liked to see the question of markets dealt with in this measure. I should like to see this council have authority to inaugurate a campaign calling on our people to buy Canadian-made goods. I should like to see a campaign carried on across the country to make sure that we have an increased home consumers' market. It is well known that any country that is dependent on exports for its existence is always in a very precarious position. Just a few years ago-the figures may be different now-it was shown that the United States was dependent on the export market for the sale of only 6 per cent of its productivity. If I remember the figures correctly, Canada was dependent on export markets for the sale of 24 per cent of its productivity. We required this market in order to keep our people employed. The crux of the situation is this, unless we have markets, unless we can sell our merchandise, no matter how efficient we are in its production, no matter how economical we are, this is only an exercise, an exploratory operation. The minister and the government should certainly address themselves to the question of markets.
I wonder whether the minister is aware of the fact that more people in this country would create and increase home consumers' market. Has any study been made by the government of markets, or will they give authority to this council to study and deal with the question of markets? Will it be done in co-operation or consultation with the Department of Trade and Commerce? I think the minister and his committee might be well advised to co-operate with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to see whether we can increase our home consumers' market so that we are not as dependent on exports as we are now.
The measure could be a useful one, but it is absolutely pointless and useless unless it indicates to us where our increased productivity and our more economical productivity

Productivity Council
will go. If we have the buyers, then I think the measure will serve a useful purpose.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to return to the point raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West and continued by the hon. member for Assiniboia and to express amazement that the hon. member for Assiniboia should have made the suggestion he did, that this bill should provide any power to the council to make recommendations to the government, because we were told by the spokesman of the Prime Minister, the parliamentary secretary, at an earlier stage in the consideration of this measure that the government needed no advice and wanted no advice, and one thing they were making sure of in this bill was that they would not get any advice.

I rise on a point of order. It is a most untrue statement to say that the Prime Minister made any such statement. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate inferred that, and this is the point of order.
I believe I have the floor. The Minister of Labour-
Don't blabber-mouth again; speak the truth.
-seems to have a curious view of debate in this house. Whenever an hon. member-
You are curious all over.
-makes a statement with which the minister disagrees, and which he has a right to disagree with when he has an opportunity to do so-
I always agree with the truth.
-he promptly rises on what he alleges is a point of order in order to interfere with the speech that is being made. I suggest that the minister, instead of abusing the rules of the house-
I don't abuse the rules; don't worry about that.
-the way he does-
I have too much respect for them.

-should listen to other hon. members and reply to them after they have finished their speeches in the ordinary way that other members of the house do. If he did that he would make much more progress in getting his legislation through the house.

I do all right. You do not have to worry about that.
[Mr. Crestohl.l

The point I am making is that the government indicated, the parliamentary secretary indicated and the Prime Minister rather indicated as well that the one thing they wanted to be sure of was that this council did not pester the government in any way.
That is not right and you know it.
Nonsense.

If they want to efface the very unfortunate impression they gave I suggest that they follow the advice of the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Assiniboia and spell out in the bill that the productivity council will have the power to make recommendations to the government, without which it will have very little value indeed.
There is no necessity to do that.

I said earlier that in our view it was necessary to extend the scope of the bill so that the council could make recommendations to the government in the field of productivity and also in the fields of employment and income. This bill is another one of those half measures-
Half-baked.
Those half-baked measures-
It is funny that all of you voted for them.
-those halting and ineffective measures introduced by the government.
We will have to call a vote on third reading again.

The government is introducing a number of bits and pieces that add up not to a program to deal with unemployment but rather to failure to deal with it. Apparently the government is really not aware of the tremendous and far-reaching unemployment situation in our country. I have in my hand today's Ottawa Journal which has this heading over an article:
Jobless Jump 61,000; Biggest Number for November in 15 Years.
The article goes on to give the exact number and percentage of unemployed. It points out that unemployment had jumped to 429,000 at mid-November. The sum total of the government's clearing away of the underbrush has been failure and the highest unemployment in Canada for any November in the last 15 years. By this legislation together with its other legislation the government underlines the fact that it does not have a comprehensive program, that it does not intend to deal with the situation, that it is turning its back on economic planning and

on adequate full employment policies. This all adds up to a government that is a complete failure and a government, I suggest, that the Canadian people can no longer afford.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two in answer to that constitutional wizard from Bonavista-Twil-lingate who last night quoted at length certain passages of my speech at the resolution stage of this measure. As he only quoted half of my remarks pertaining to whether this was an advisory body or whatever else it might be, I think it is only fair that I should put the whole of my remarks pertaining to that particular point on the record now, and I intend to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am afraid that the committee is rehashing second reading of the bill. We are now on clause 1 and are supposed to be considering the details of the clauses of the bill. I must suggest to the hon. member that he abide by the rules.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to rise on the point of order you have raised in defence of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue. We have been discussing all afternoon the powers of the council and this is the point that is before us now. The hon. member feels that he was improperly misrepresented by another hon. member and I think he should be allowed to state his position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
On the point of order, the passage I wish to quote simply deals with the powers that the council may have and, viewed in that respect, I respectfully submit that it is pertinent to the present discussion. The hon. wizard-I mean the hon. member-had reached this point in quoting my remarks, and I read from page 720 of Hansard of December 12:
The resolution is of a technical nature. The policy of the government is to promote greater economic activity in all phases of our nation. One of its purposes in particular will be to promote and increase productivity in industry, manufacturing and other pursuits. So we are faced with a technical body. That is why there is no difference and no inconsistency whatsoever between the position then taken and the position now being taken by this government by the introduction of this resolution.
Then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked me whether I would permit a question, to which I replied, "Yes, certainly." The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked this question:
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that since the earlier proposal was for an advisory council, in his opinion the present government needed no advice in formulating policy?
Productivity Council
To which I replied as follows, and this is the point that I hope will sink into the hon. head of the hon. member:
As usual, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate displays an astonishing difficulty in comprehending even the simplest proposition. What I said was that the government does not need a body to indicate to it what policies it should adopt, that under our democratic process policymaking is the special and reserved field of the government. But having adopted a policy, and that policy being greater productivity, it is in the execution of that over-all policy that it now calls upon this house to approve the present resolution. It is as simple as that and no amount of twisting or apparent misapprehension on the part of the hon. member will change the clarity of that particular statement.
That is quite true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Viewed in that light I think it should be a complete answer to the point raised by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask leave-I have been on my feet three times -to put this question. When will the 429,000 jobless, to whom reference was just made, have an answer as to the effect of the bill, which has arisen out of a conference to meet the problem of unemployment, in creating jobs? In particular I would ask the Minister of Labour or the hon. gentleman opposite whether any of the individuals to be appointed have been approached or whether any of the groups concerned, industry, commerce, labour and agriculture, have been approached. Has there been any investigation made by the government as to the individuals who will be named in order that we may have a date when the productivity council will begin to function? This would at least be the first stage from which any benefits to the jobless could conceivably begin to flow.

Mr. Chairman, of course I do not imagine that the hon. member for Niagara Falls really thought I would say that this bill would solve the problem of unemployment for the whole 429,000 people at once. I am sure that since she has been in this house and has participated in the voting on the various measures this government has introduced, and given her approval of them as measures to combat unemployment, she realizes that this and other measures that will be brought down are part and parcel of a program to take care of the federal share of responsibility in this field and which will create an atmosphere that will give employment to these people.
In so far as the second part of the question is concerned, I may say that just as soon as royal assent is given to this bill steps will

Productivity Council
be taken to communicate with people about the organization of this productivity council without any loss of time.

I take it then from what the Minister of Labour says that this bill is not designed to create jobs or immediately alleviate unemployment for the 429,000 or any part thereof, and that there has been misrepresentation to the public at large about the scope fo this measure and its goal?

In order that the hon. lady will not be under any misapprehension or be misinformed, may I say this is one of the measures that will bring about a solution of the unemployment problem affecting these 429,000 people.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to pursue the questions raised by the hon. lady. In doing so, I should like to refer to the statements made by the Prime Minister yesterday in moving second reading of the bill in order to obtain certain clarifications from the minister as to the meaning of some of the things that the Prime Minister said. It seems to me this is a reasonable thing to ask in committee. Some of these statements are not any clearer than I found the clarity of the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, whose clarity I think still leaves something to be desired.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: It takes time to sink in.

It sank without a trace. At page 750 of Hansard for yesterday we find the conclusion of the Prime Minister's speech on second reading in which he indicated there were two goals for this measure. This is the third paragraph, and I do not want to read the whole paragraph, but I am quite willing to do so if it is insisted upon. I am going to try to shorten it without, I hope, doing any injustice to the statement. He referred to two objectives, the assurance of the preservation of our standard of living and, at the same time, the maintenance at the lowest possible minimum, the costs of production. Then he said:
The achievement of both can be attained through the advances of technological skill.
This next sentence is the one with which I am particularly concerned.
Concomitant with that we require to have the best opinion available about how to use technological advances not only for the attainment of those objectives-
I direct the minister's attention particularly to the next few words.
-but in order not to deny those who should have work the right and opportunity of having it.
That is the purpose of this legislation.
Let me repeat what the Prime Minister states is the real purpose of this legislation.

The purpose of this legislation is not to deny those who should have work the right and opportunity of having it. Would the minister explain just how this legislation is going to guard against the denial to those who should have work the right and opportunity of having it?
And when.
And when.

I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has been busy reading manuscripts on his desk and clippings while certain statements were being made here because on two occasions at least I have outlined the experience in the United Kingdom, for example. As a result of the efficiency brought about in industry there labour was assured of its place. Costs were reduced through the better use of fuel, machinery and material without undermining the jobs available in that industry. The reduction of costs rather created more jobs in industry, and that is what we are after. We want to have all these people working together, industry and labour, to bring about efficiency, a reduction in the cost of our products, the result of which will be a more competitive product for the export market. Then, the more we need to produce, the more jobs will be created. I think even the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would not argue against an objective of that sort.

No, I did not argue with it. If the minister had been listening to what I said yesterday on second reading he would have found that I agreed precisely with that as a long term objective, and that is the only reason we are voting for this bill at all. We do believe it has a reasonable long term objective. However, I want to remind the minister, who talks about all these jobs that were assured in the United Kingdom, that in the United Kingdom they have had full employment continuously since the war. The only year in which there has been any considerable amount of unemployment has been the year 1960, and this productivity council has been in operation in the United Kingdom since 1948. The plain fact is that the productivity council was never set up to deal with the unemployment problem at all. It was set up to deal with an entirely different problem, namely the problem of making the best possible use of scarce manpower, not the problem of surplus manpower. To fob off this as a measure to deal with unemployment is a farce and a fiction, if I may adopt that word which was made parliamentary by the right hon. gentleman last night.
I want to draw the minister's attention to the very next words of the Prime Minister

because the minister said I was reading various manuscripts. I was not reading manuscripts, I was reading the Prime Minister's speech and trying to find out if any meaning could be found in it what the meaning was. I really defy any person who has any knowledge of the English language to find any meaning in the first speech that was made by the Prime Minister yesterday. The second speech, which had nothing to do with the bill, had plenty of meaning and a good deal of feeling. However, in the first speech in which the Prime Minister pretended to be dealing with the bill, so far as I can find out there was no clear meaning of any kind. I ask the minister to tell us precisely what is meant by the next sentence-I will read two sentences:
That is the purpose of this legislation. It is a segment of the policy we are bringing before the house bill by bill.
These segments, are like one of those jigsaw puzzles with some of the pieces missing and the Prime Minister tells us they are going to be missing until he sees fit to bring them down. The Canadian people, therefore, are not to be told what is the whole plan. It will be let out bit by bit, piece by piece, making a headline this week and another headline next week and another headline the week after, instead of the whole thing being disclosed honestly and in a straightforward manner in an effort to solve the problem instead of creating additional advertising which is the greatest lack of the present government according to its head. I see the chairman is getting restive, so I had better come back to the sentence
What was your question?

I want the minister to elucidate the next sentence.
This policy, we believe, will be beneficial not only in the short term but in the longer term as well,-
The minister has told us two or three times about the longer term and as far as I know there is no disagreement in the house about the longer term. But I wish the minister would tell us what this bill is going to accomplish in the short term.

If the hon. member reads
Hansard tomorrow he will see the answer I gave when I was replying to members who had previously asked a question on this subj ect.
Would the minister say whether in the short term it is the opinion of the government that the setting up of this council will have any effect at all on the level of employment?

More than 21 years.
90205-6-524
Productivity Council
I feel certain that through cooperation with this productivity council results can be brought about-and, I think, notable results-in the next six months. Is that the long term or the short term?

I would regard that as the short term. This being December 14, if we are still here on June 14 and if it is a sitting day I will make a note to ask the minister to give us in detail the short term results that have been achieved by this council in that time.
You are stupid enough to ask a question like that, aren't you?
Yes, I am stupid enough to stick to facts and I am not ashamed of that form of stupidity.
Some facts. They are what you call facts.

The hon. gentlemen do not seem to like what is being said about this bill. I would like the minister to explain another sentence of the Prime Minister's remarks, because I must say this one completely baffled me.
It is no good, eh?

This is what the Prime Minister is reported as having said on page 749 of Hansard. This is the Prime Minister speaking about this council, this bill:
I would hope that the basic technique would be to direct the public consciousness not to fear but to faith; not to pointing out the difficulties without suggesting solutions, but to pointing to the strength and vigour of Canada and to bringing about, in a unity of effort, the best consideration that the best minds of Canada can bring to this problem.
Would the minister tell us just precisely how this faith-healing operation is going to be carried on by this council?

Why do you not ask the
Prime Minister?

Does the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate feel that the people who will be appointed to this council, who will be recommended by labour, who will be recommended by industry and others have not the ability to do some of the things that possibly he alone could do to bring about some results?

We would all like to find out what these people are going to do and what to expect of them when they are appointed, because anybody who reads this bill, with its vague language, does not know what this will be.
Of course, the bill has nearly every kind of vagueness in it except a tribute to motherhood, but when it comes to getting down to

Productivity Council
brass tacks and dealing with providing jobs for people who have not jobs, you have to have a more powerful microscope than anyone in the house, including the minister, seems yet to have been able to employ to find any trace of any device that would operate in that regard. Yet we are told it is part of the program to solve unemployment.

I have probably, and I am sure I am right, a great deal more faith in the ingenuity and ability of Canadians than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In my experience I have found that when representative Canadians are asked to serve on bodies, whether they are set up by the federal government, provincial governments or municipal governments, they usually have pretty good ingenuity in bringing about favourable results. Through this bill we think these people will be able, through their Canadian ingenuity

which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has no faith in, evidently-to do a good job for Canadians, for Canadian industry, for Canadian labour, for Canada generally.

Mr. Chairman, I have been endeavouring to get the floor for some little time to state that the minister has alleviated a few of my misgivings about this bill, but unfortunately I did not get up in time. I find that now in at least one respect we are pretty nearly back to where we started.
I understood the minister to admit quite frankly that there really was not too much immediate benefit to be obtained from this bill, but it would be a very beneficial thing in the long term. Certainly my objections on that particular basis have been alleviated. But I now find that the minister has reversed himself slightly and expects some considerable benefit within the next six months.
The second point on which the minister has somewhat alleviated my concern is this. He stated it is his understanding that there will be recommendations from this council. There again there is certainly a new method being adopted here, where the council is going to have permission by omission to make these recommendations.
The third point that I was very glad to hear the minister make was that, contrary to what might have been interpreted from the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, this bill is not solely for the benefit of industry.
However, there is one point that I do not think has yet received enough consideration. That has to do with tax exemptions or, not putting it so kindly perhaps, to tax evasion

that will be favourable to companies which contribute to this council. This is a particular point I would like to make.
If companies are able to write off normal tax assessments in this manner it means that the taxes they are writing off will have to be raised from some other source. The only people in the country who have not some means of writing off income tax are the poor wage earners who have their tax deducted at source. Therefore this means that every time a company finds another method of getting out of paying tax, the taxes have to be raised that much more by these people who have no opportunity of getting out of paying taxes. It takes so many dollars to run the country, regardless of the source from which they are raised.
I am not too happy about the aspect of this bill, which is in fact an inducement, or will be an inducement to companies and other organizations to further evade paying tax. But there is still one further point in this connection. Not only is the wage earner going to have his taxes raised because he will be affected in this manner, but in addition he is going to have to match that tax evasion. This is certainly a brand new principle and I would like to see if the minister would agree that this is completely unfair, or it is possibly pushing things a little too far?
I do not really know what the hon. member is talking about when he talks about tax evasion. I see nothing in this bill that has anything to do with tax evasion of any kind.

I am referring to clause 16 of the bill, under which any company or organization which contributes to this council will receive the benefits of the Income Tax Act which will permit that as a deduction from income tax. In addition to that I am pointing to the fact that this money will not go in taxes and will have to be raised elsewhere, that the taxpayer is being asked to match this tax exemption.

This is standard legislation where tax deductions are allowable when donations are made to certain organizations which come under exemption for income tax. Most certainly I think this is a worth-while effort on the part of anyone to which to donate and it should be recognized in the same way in this instance, because if any benefit is going to be derived from these donations because of the function of this productivity council they are certainly entitled to the same consideration. Most certainly, in my opinion, there is no tax evasion when this procedure is followed.
This is a budgetary item.

The minister has missed the second part of my point, that under the provisions of this bill, in addition to the normal situation where donations of this kind are tax exempt, the taxpayers of Canada are being asked to match these amounts. It is double inducement.

Mr. Chairman, I have one further question that perhaps the Minister of Labour will answer.
Last night, listening to the Prime Minister discuss in a fairly general way the purport of this bill, I heard him say, with some astonishment and great interest, what is referred to on page 749 of Hansard when he was discussing the question of research. This is one part of the scope of the council as set up in this bill. In the third paragraph, about the middle of the page, the right hon. gentleman said:
Indeed, I express the hope that foreign concerns with subsidiaries in Canada will make available in Canada a major portion of the proportionate share that the Canadian industry bears to the total production of the entire industry and that this amount will be devoted to research rather than having the research done in another country, the course followed today.
My particular interest arises from the fact that in my riding all but about two companies are Canadian subsidiaries of foreign concerns, generally from one particular country, and I should like to ask the Minister of Labour whether the government has any reason to believe that such diversion of expenditure to answer unemployment in their own country will be made to their Canadian subsidiaries, and whether any assurances have been given and, if so, what assurances, by these companies; and, further, if there is anything in the bill which gives this council any authority whatsoever over United States, Swiss, British, German or other head offices outside this country, or whether this is just a pious hope.

I do not think it is fair to ask me what the Prime Minister meant by this. He probably has had communications, or has some knowledge of it. I do not have knowledge of any company outside the boundaries of Canada which has made any promises. I do not know of any. I think it is only right that the hon. lady should address this question to the Prime Minister when he is here, and not wait until he has left.

I did not wait until he left. I protest that had he been here I would still have asked him. I well recognize that it must be somewhat difficult for even so close a colleague as the Minister of Labour to understand what the Prime Minister has in mind on occasions. However, 1 did ask another
Productivity Council
question as to whether there is any provision in this bill by means of which this council would have any control or right to interfere in matters which deal with head offices outside Canada.
No, there is not.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Establishment of Council.

I have a few words to say on one aspect of this bill, which is of tremendous importance to the district of Nipissing, in connection with clause 2, the clause which provides for the establishment of the council and, in particular with its composition as set out in subclauses (a) to (f).
It is my sincere hope that the government will take this opportunity to appoint an outstanding authority from the railroad industry to this council, because it seems to me there are few sections of industry in Canada today which are running more contrary to the stated objectives of this bill than are the railways. This bill talks in clause 10(a) (iii) about the maintenance of good human relations and, in the next sub paragraph, about the use of training programs at all levels of industry. Subparagraph (v) speaks about the use of retraining programs to meet changing manpower requirements.
I know something of this problem, coming as I do from a community which has been an important railroad centre since its very establishment; in fact, its development was brought about, I might say, because of the construction of a railroad. The North Bay area is an important C.P.R. point and there is considerable activity by the Canadian National Railways. It is also the southern terminus of the Ontario Northland railway. Almost every week for the last two years I have had someone in to see me seeking assistance in relocating or re-establishing himself after being laid off from one of these roads.
Here we have people who went directly from school to the railroads. Most of them have worked hard to improve their positions. Through the years they have taken courses, recommended by their companies, that would further equip them to do the job they were doing. Suddenly, like lightning, the situation is all changed. On the fifteenth of a month notice may be received that their employment will terminate perhaps on the thirtieth of that month. Certainly this is scarcely in keeping with the objectives outlined in this bill.
I had five men in to see me recently who had worked for the railroad for approximately 40 years and who were then abruptly dropped from the payroll. These men, who had begun to work for the railroads early in life, have

Productivity Council
many useful years for employment ahead of them despite their long service. A situation of this kind is bad enough, but what about the younger man? He has so much more of his life left. In many cases he has been doing the same job, say for 30 years since he left school. If he left school when he was 17 today he would be 47, still a comparatively young man. In the situation which exists today, finding himself untrained for other work, where can he turn? Without belabouring this point, it seems to me there is no better example than among the railways of action which would seem to be completely contrary to the Prime Minister's interpretation of the objectives of this bill.
Most Canadians are aware that our railways are passing through a difficult period at the present time, but surely, and this is especially true of the Canadian National over which this government must have some influence, in the interest of all concerned the Canadian National should be setting an example in respect to the retraining and relocation of personnel being laid off. Here the Canadian National could take the lead and I am sure it would be followed, at least to some degree, by other railroads.
Coming as I do from a railroad centre I know that the morale of the men employed has been steadily weakened by this apparent lack of interest and the apparent inaction by both management and government with regard to helping men who have been laid off to secure satisfactory alternative employment. I would hope that this government might give the fullest possible consideration to making sure that this important industry, which admittedly is passing through a difficult transition period, is well represented in the membership of this national productivity council.
I do not wish to delay the committee by giving details, but I can assure hon. members that there is a great need for action in this field, action which would improve the human relations aspect of the industry, a field with which this bill purports to deal. Few industries in Canada need more informed and considered attention than the railways in effecting successfully the transition made necessary by automation. For this reason I make this request directly to the minister and the government-that they should appoint a competent railroad authority to this council in order to ensure that the further automation of our railroads may result in the minimum amount of dislocation and technological unemployment.

Further to what my hon. friend has said I would refer to a report in the Toronto Telegram which I understand supports hon. gentlemen opposite. It is dated

October 25 and refers to the statement that this body, when set up, will contain representatives of industry, labour, agriculture, the Canadian Legion, the universities, women's organizations and the government.
Certainly I would suggest that these various bodies, and particularly, the women's organizations, would know a great deal about productivity and would be able to assist the government on being appointed to such a board. However, I see when the bill is produced that these groups which have indicated from time to time a tremendous interest in public affairs both of the day and of the future have been cavalierly dropped. I would ask the Minister of Labour for what reason they were not included and whether the government might reconsider the question of having appointed representatives of each of the groups included in the paragraphs of clause 2?
There is provision under paragraph (d) for the appointment of five members from the general public. I would remind the hon. lady that women are also in industry, commerce and in the professions.

How would the Canadian Legion and universities fit into that category? Specific reference was made to them in the announcement of the Prime Minister at a time when he was prepared to bring a bill before us but these are not reflected in clause 2.	[DOT]
They will be considered. The appointment of representatives from those groups will be considered when we make the appointment under paragraph (d) of five members of the general public.

Mr. Chairman, the minister in speaking in the house the day before yesterday at an earlier stage in the consideration of this measure made specific reference, as may be found at page 733 of Hansard, to industry, labour and universities being included. I note that the provisions for universities has not been included in this clause although the other groups the minister referred to were obviously based on his reference to this clause because they are included by identical reference. Was any consideration given to the question of the appointment of representatives of the universities as such?
They will be represented as one of the five members of the general public.

I believe I put a more precise question than that. In his speech the minister obviously referred to the categories in clause 2 of the bill with the exception

that he included universities as if it were one of the categories and in the bill before us no such reference is included. The Prime Minister in his newspaper reference did the same thing. Was there any particular reason why universities are not being included when the public, from the press statement of the Prime Minister, and in the house, from the statement of the minister, would have every reason to expect that they were being included?

Mr. Chairman, I was speaking on the resolution stage then. There was no bill before us at the time. We could not set out each and every group in particular but we did provide for the appointment of five members from the general public and we feel that the representation referred to by the hon. gentleman could be included.

I would have hoped that the minister would have been familiar with a bill when at the resolution stage he was asking the house to bring the measure before it for consideration. I would point out that his statement does lead one to believe that he was dealing at the resolution stage with groups that would be specifically included.
Did the hon. member really get that impression?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. So there will be no doubt about it the reference is page 733 of Hansard. During the time I was listening to the minister I thought he was improving on the remarks made by his colleague who presented the resolution to the house.
I must point out to the minister that we have already had three ministers of the crown present this measure at different stages. The Minister of Trade and Commerce presented it at one stage so we looked to the hon. gentleman's speech for guidance on the subject. The Prime Minister presented the measure for second reading and in turn we looked to his pronouncement for guidance on the subject. The Minister of Labour is piloting the measure at this time. I am content enough that the hon. gentleman is doing so but I would point out to him that there are these several statements which are confusing to both the public and hon. members of the committee. Certainly the announcement of the Prime Minister at the conclusion of the conference on unemployment was of such a nature that it may have misled a great portion of the public. One of the smaller points on which it is confusing is the hon. gentleman's reference to business, industry, labour, agriculture and education, as reported in one paper, and his reference to universities, as reported in another, and the minister's own
Productivity Council
statement in this chamber in setting out the groups that would comprise the council in which specifically included universities.

I did not say they would be represented or that any group would be represented. Referring to my remarks as found at page 733 of Hansard of December 12, I said:
I am sure that the collective knowledge, the skills and the experience of commerce, industry, labour, universities, government and of citizens generally is needed at this time.
Most certainly this council is going to confer with universities and everyone else who shows any interest in an effort to bring about the objectives we hope will be brought about through the establishment of this council.

Let me put one more question to the minister. If the minister is sure that the collective knowledge of the universities, among other groups, is needed at this time, why does he not provide for the appointment on the council of representatives of the universities as such?
There is provision for their appointment in the reference to the appointment of five members of the general public.

The minister just said that the provision for the five members of the general public would take care of the representatives of women's organizations and the Canadian Legion in answer to my hon. colleague's question, and now he refers to universities.
This will not take up the whole five.
But it does not leave many for what most hon. members would understand by the words "general public".

Mr. Chairman, we have already expressed very serious doubt as to the immediate effectiveness of this measure in terms of promoting employment so my remarks will be brief. Since the government has its own views on the matter the only alternative we have at this stage is to see that this bill is improved as much as possible.
I understand that clause 2 relates to the appointment of the council. I am wondering if it is the intention of the government to see that the ten provinces are represented on this board. If so, would it not be a good thing that mention be made of this intention in clause 2? Since we are dealing here with a national council on a national scale I think the ten provinces should be represented and if they are mention of this should be made in clause 2.

Productivity Council

There is no provision for the representation of the provinces on the council. I wish to point out, however, that a number of the provincial governments already carry out some work in this field. It is anticipated, and I am sure the anticipation will be realized, that the national productivity council will co-operate fully with these provincial bodies, both governmental and private.

Perhaps the minister misunderstood me, Mr. Chairman. I had in mind that the membership of the council should be drawn from among people residing in all of the ten provinces thus giving full provincial representation in that sense of the word.
I see what the hon. member means now.

Paragraph (c) of clause 2 states that membership of the council will include five members who will be chosen from the fields of agriculture and other primary industries. My question to the minister is this. Will the fishing industry be recognized as one of the primary industries to be represented?
Yes.
May I ask a question? Do the words "industry and commerce" in paragraph (a) include finance or exclude it?
Yes.
May I ask the minister how you improve the productivity of finance?
You slay me.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3-Appointment of executive director.

Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure the minister did not draft subclause 5 of clause 3. Perhaps it is not too important, except we are legislating on something that is obviously impossible, or may be impossible. The minister is saying:
A person in order to be eligible to be appointed as a member of the council described in paragraph (a),	(b),	(c) or (e) of section 2 shall have
knowledge of the field he is to represent and of productivity problems related to that field, or shall have knowledge of technical aspects of industrial productivity.
I do not know how the minister is going to settle the question of a man's ability or his degree of knowledge. Probably it is relatively innocuous but certainly it adds nothing to the bill. It could be reduced to an absurdity if one were disposed to do it. For instance, there is the requirement under (c) that a person to be eligible for appointment, assuming he has knowledge of the field of agriculture, and to be chosen must not only have knowledge of agriculture but he must also have knowledge

of other primary industries. I think the thing reduces itself to an absurdity. I do not propose to pursue the argument other than to point out to the minister a subclause that should not be in there in its present form.

The language of subparagraph (5) also struck me as it did the hon. member for Ottawa West. When in law you say that a person has to be eligible for a certain appointment, this eligibility has to be determined somehow. My question to the minister is, how will eligibility be decided? Will these gentlemen be subjected to an examination to see whether they are eligible or qualified for the appointment? It might have another meaning to say that a man has to be eligible to receive an appointment. Does the minister envisage submitting these gentlemen to an examination to see whether they are really eligible for the appointment?

No, of course not. I think we can easily pick people with practical experience, those engaged in the business world, in the manufacturing world, in plants, in factories, representing labour, who have practical knowledge of the production of those materials. That is all we will need. That is the qualification that will be needed.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 4 agreed to.
On clause 5-Salary of executive director.

Mr. Chairman, I see that an honorarium of $3,000 is to be paid to the chairman but I find it strange that no fixed amount is set for the executive director. This strikes me as a bit of an anomaly. Can the minister explain it?
A blank cheque.

Of course, the executive director will be a full-time employee, and his salary will be set by the governor in council. You do not want to amend the bill every time you wish to give the man an increase in wages, surely.
How is it done in other measures? There are other appointments made by statute in which the maximum salary is fixed. Why this wide open thing?
That varies, sir.

I think the minister may have made a slip when he was dealing with the executive director. I think he said he would be paid an amount by the governor in council, but it is paid by the productivity council.
The salary will be fixed by the governor in council.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 6 to 9, inclusive, agreed to.
On clause 10-Objects and powers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This clause of the bill sets out the objectives and powers of the legislation. We believe that many of the things that the minister says can be accomplished, can be accomplished only if there is a further addition to this clause of the bill. The desire is not only to increase productivity but also to sell the products. In every country where councils have been successful, and in our own country, it has always been necessary to find some method of disposing of the goods that are produced. That is why the productivity councils were so successful in the years after the war and also during the war period when there was a great need and an extended market for goods. It has been necessary to have this not only in fields where there is no need to create employment but where there is unemployment. This has been tried in such countries as West Germany, where the productivity on a national basis was geared to the marketing of the products. I am told that before the products were even produced in West Germany they produced prototypes of the products of their industry and then proceeded to find markets for them. They brought the orders home, and then set their factories in production and in this manner they were able to take care of the employment situation as well as productivity. It seems to me that the marketing of the product is as important as increasing productivity. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That subparagraph (i) of paragraph (a) of clause 10 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"(i) the development of improved production, marketing, and distribution methods,"
It seems to me that if we are to concentrate on the problem of producing products and make this part of the over-all aims and aspirations of the productivity council we should go out and market the products as we get them. If we do this then we shall be doing some good. If we are to develop only further automation for the sake of being able to work for machines, then I am not in favour of it. If we are interested only in increased production, then I say we are not solving some of the problems we have, and we shall not be attaining the objectives which the minister indicates are contained in this bill.
I should like to use several examples. We have increased productivity in the pulp and
Productivity Council
paper industry; we have increased productivity in the steel industry. My colleague has said that we have increased productivity particularly in the farming industry. In each case we have been unable to go out and sell the products of that increased productivity. In many instances this has resulted in a lessening of employment and activity in these particular fields. In only one of them has any decrease in price resulted because of increased productivity and that is in the field of agriculture where it can be ill afforded. In some cases we have decreased the price of a product and have paid a subsidy to the people engaged in that industry. This does not appear to be a satisfactory way of doing it. Unless we are willing to institute a concentrated marketing program, I think this measure will not serve the interests that the minister says it is meant to serve.
Amendment (Mr. Peters) negatived: Yeas, 17; nays, 41.

Mr. Chairman, clause 10 sets forth a number of commendable objects and powers but its main emphasis is on the improvement of technical efficiency. Even if we do achieve our objective as to technical efficiency it does not follow that the benefits accruing from that will be used to serve the national interests in the best way. For example, we may produce a lot of things which do not serve the greatest public need. I have always felt that a body of this kind should be set up to keep a watchful eye over the variations in productivity trends from time to time and also to ensure that we get the best maximum use out of the materials that are used. Other members have also intimated today that the objects and powers of the council should be enlarged. I made similar remarks last night and without repeating the arguments I have already placed on Hansard I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River:
That paragraph (a) of clause 10 be amended by deleting the word "and" at the end of line 24 and adding the following:
(viii) The sponsoring of periodic meetings between representatives of industry, labour and consumers for the purpose of appraising productivity trends and determining what changes, if any, are desirable to best serve the national interest; and, at the same time, ensure the maximum utilization of our resources by all possible means, including the elimination of unnecessary waste of material on features and refinements which have no practical value. To publish reports of all such meetings; and.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

Before the vote is taken I should like to commend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. This is one of the best C.C.F. amendments I have seen for a long time and I can assure him of our full support.

Productivity Council

Surely this second amendment to this clause is not going to be voted down without some expression of opinion from the minister. The amendment seems to have a great deal of merit and not in any way to offend the purposes of the legislation as outlined by the government. Certainly the committee would want to give the minister full time to examine the text as it is somewhat lengthy. In view of the merit and purposes of the amendment I do not think it should be simply ignored and voted down just because one side has a massive majority in the house.

Certainly that is not the case. The fact is that in clause 10 (b) we provide for that opportunity. I also want to remind the hon. member that we do live in a free economy and there is nothing to prevent labour, management or all other sectors of the community from getting together and working out a solution of their problems.
Amendment (Mr. Carter) negatived: Yeas, 18; nays, 51.

Mr. Chairman, we do not seem to be having too much success in our endeavours to improve the bill. However, I am sure the amendment I intend to move now will receive much more support from the other side of the house than has been the case so far. In fact, the minister has already expressed his endorsation of the spirit of this amendment.
It appears to me, Mr. Chairman, that there is one grave weakness in this bill. This measure establishes a productivity council which is going to have at its disposal a vast amount of information. It should have a very thorough knowledge of the subjects with which it will be dealing, and yet there is no provision in this bill for this knowledge that has been gathered coming back to this house or even to the government in the form of recommendations. I feel this is a very serious omission. With that in mind, I should like to move:
That the clause be amended by adding the following as paragraph (c):
"(c) make recommendations which are deemed necessary to give effect to any of the objects described in this section."

Unfortunately, I have been detained on very urgent business this afternoon but I am glad I have arrived back in time to support this very sensible amendment proposed by the hon. member for Timmins. I thought the reasons he gave for the amendment were quite valid and substantial, in view of the fact that this council will have this mass of information. In a sense, it will have information at its fingertips in the same fashion as a royal commission. I

cannot see why this council, in view of its close association with the facts, should not have the power to make recommendations to the government in much the same way as the royal commission on transportation would do. I, therefore, support this amendment and if the government does not see fit to accept it I should like to hear the minister's explanation because the hon. member for Timmins rather intimated the minister had accepted it in principle.
The hon. member should not take the word of the hon. member for Timmins.

I should like the minister to inform the committee why such an amendment is not acceptable, and why a council like this which is obtaining all this information should be denied the opportunity to make recommendations. Why has it not the same right as that given to royal commissions?

I am inclined to agree with some of the things the hon. member has said, but I am not able to follow all that he has said. Does he suggest that unless this amendment is passed this means that in some way all the information which the council will have will just have to remain inactive and passive? I am sure the minister will be able to explain that that is not the case.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In connection with this
amendment which has just been moved I think the committee should recall the statement that was made by the Prime Minister during the course of the debate, and give heed and consideration to it. Yesterday, at page 750 of Hansard, the Prime Minister is reported as saying this:
I shall have more to say after the house has had the benefit of the opinions of hon. members in connection with this matter. I know we shall welcome any ideas or suggestions that may lead to any improvement in the bill, providing those suggestions are not of such a nature as would, in effect, constitute the council as a policy-making body with any control over the government. This, after all, would simply be applied socialism, and we, believing in private enterprise, will not accept suggestions of that type. But if there are views or ideas that will contribute to the strengthening of the objective and powers of the council or which in any way, in the opinion of the government, add to or strengthen the likelihood of attaining the objectives we have in mind, we shall be most happy to have the benefit of those ideas.
I would say, in these circumstances, we have been submitting to the government a number of ideas which are constructive and are in the nature of the words used by the Prime Minister last night. The Prime Minister is now coming into the chamber, and I ask him if this amendment is not of the kind and character that he had in mind last evening. It does not change the nature of

the clause but it does expand it. It certainly could not do any harm. In view of what the Prime Minister has said, I suggest to him and those who sit with him that this amendment be accepted.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has correctly quoted what the Prime Minister said yesterday. However, in looking at this amendment I want to refer again to clause 10. It does not limit the work of the council in respect of any recommendations. This clause says that without limiting the generality of the foregoing the council may in furtherance of its objects, foster and promote, and then there is a list of things.
As I pointed out before, there is nothing in this clause that forbids the council making recommendations to the federal government if it feels the federal government can be of some help. The council can make recommendations to anyone else. We feel that within the provisions of the bill the productivity council can make recommendations and this amendment, therefore, does not make any change at all.
Does the minister interpret clause 10 as meaning that the council can make recommendations on policy matters?

The hon. member is straying away again, and we will have to bring him back into the corral. I shall have to repeat everything I have said. With the co-operation of labour and other interested groups it will be the duty of this council to work out the problems of efficiency and higher productivity, taking into consideration the human element. Most certainly they will make recommendations to industry, to labour and to the government or anyone they feel needs to participate in bringing about its objectives.
Business of the House

I think the minister chose a very apt word in describing this clause. It is very much a corral, and that is exactly what he has done to this productivity council. He has a good idea here in setting up the productivity council, but he is rendering it powerless to do the kind of job that it would otherwise be able to do in making industry in this country more efficient by limiting the powers in clause 10 unduly and improperly.
You put sheep in a corral.

Six o'clock.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what we will be doing tomorrow and Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow, we will continue to study Bill No. C-52 in the committee stage, followed by supplementary estimates. Depending on the progress made tomorrow I will announce the business for Friday. If this bill is completed and the supplementary estimates are finished, on Friday we will have the continuation of the resolution stage of the measure dealing with veterans' pensions, and then the resolution dealing with the agricultural development program.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could we have some indication of what the house will be doing on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What is unfinished of that program on Friday will be carried forward to Monday.
